paragraphs.heading: Programmed cell death
paragraphs.text: Apoptosis is a form of programmed cell death. It happens in multicellular organisms and in some single-celled eukaryotes such as yeast. The name comes from the Greek for falling off, as leaves fall from a tree. A series of biochemical events produces characteristic changes before death: the cell shrinks and forms blebs, its chromatin condenses, its nucleus and DNA break into fragments, and its mRNA decays.

paragraphs.heading: Why the body needs it
paragraphs.text: Necrosis is traumatic cell death caused by acute injury; apoptosis, by contrast, is highly regulated and brings advantages over an organism's life. For example, the fingers and toes of a developing human embryo separate because the cells between them go through a genetically determined form of apoptosis. A dying cell breaks into pieces called apoptotic bodies, which phagocytes engulf and remove before the cell's contents can spill out and damage nearby cells. The scale is large: an average adult loses 50 to 70 billion cells a day this way, and a child aged 8 to 14 loses about 20 to 30 billion.

paragraphs.heading: Two pathways to the same end
paragraphs.text: Once apoptosis starts it cannot be stopped and always ends in the cell's death, so its start is tightly regulated. Of the two best-understood routes, one is intrinsic (also known as mitochondrial) and the other extrinsic. The intrinsic route is set off by stress the cell detects in itself, though weak outside signals can also trigger it. The extrinsic route is set off by signals that come from other cells. Both switch on caspases, enzymes that break down proteins: initiator caspases activate executioner caspases, which then degrade proteins indiscriminately and kill the cell.

paragraphs.heading: When it goes wrong
paragraphs.text: Faulty apoptosis has been linked to a wide variety of diseases. Too much of it causes atrophy, while too little leads to uncontrolled multiplication of cells, such as cancer. Some factors, like Fas receptors and caspases, push cells toward apoptosis, and some proteins of the Bcl-2 family hold it back. In 1988, BCL2, the gene behind follicular lymphoma, was shown to code for a protein that blocks cell death, which tied faulty cell death to human disease, cancer in particular.

paragraphs.heading: Discovery and a name
paragraphs.text: The German scientist Carl Vogt first described the principle of apoptosis in 1842, and the anatomist Walther Flemming gave a more precise account in 1885, but the subject was not revived until 1965. John Kerr of the University of Queensland, looking at tissue under an electron microscope, told apoptosis apart from traumatic cell death. In 1972 Kerr, Andrew Wyllie and Alastair Currie published a key paper in the British Journal of Cancer that called the process apoptosis, a word they credited to James Cormack, a Greek professor at the University of Aberdeen. In 2002 Sydney Brenner, H. Robert Horvitz and John Sulston won the Nobel Prize in Medicine for finding genes that control apoptosis in the nematode C. elegans, genes whose human counterparts also regulate it.
